::: {.page-intro}
A new course on **high-performance computing in Julia**, aimed at third-year **ENSAI** students who
are comfortable in Python but new to Julia. The guiding idea: speed doesn't come from the
language itself but from understanding what the machine actually does — cost per operation, data movement,
and sharing. **Python is the familiar point of comparison; Julia is the test bench.**
:::


A single **running example** runs through the course — estimating **π by Monte-Carlo** — carried from a
plain sequential loop, to multithreading, to the GPU.

## Three sessions, nine hours

1. **Measure before optimizing** — warmup, timing, π, short dispatch introduction; compilation and diagnostic activities.
2. **Overlap waits, split computation** — I/O, races, local counts and reduction; I/O and CPU-parallel activities.
3. **Move less data** — locality, batching, CPU/GPU decisions; locality, batching and GPU activities.

[Detailed 3 × 180-minute plan, activity instructions and expected outputs](sessions.qmd).
Activities take **20–30 minutes**, including prediction, implementation and interpretation; the plan reserves debriefs and breaks.

**Before class (20–30 minutes):** open a Python notebook and run a small sum. Know functions,
loops, lists, NumPy arrays and matrix-vector products. No Julia, asyncio or CUDA prerequisite.
Colab avoids local installation; for local Python install `numpy numba matplotlib threadpoolctl`.
The GPU notebook also uses `torch`. Python CPU notebooks need the supplied
[worker module](python/parallel_workers.py), placed beside a standalone downloaded notebook.
Julia is optional: prepare `BenchmarkTools` and `UnicodePlots`; add `CUDA` only for GPU/reference notebooks.
Use the CPU-only activities for locality without CUDA. Pluto manages its own packages.

## Modules

```{=html}
<div class="aurora-card-grid">
  <div class="aurora-card">
    <span class="aurora-card__icon">🔰</span>
    <span class="aurora-card__title">0 · Julia for Python users</span>
    <span class="aurora-card__desc">Just enough Julia to read the running example: the Monte-Carlo π loop, <code>end</code>, 1-based ranges, the dot, macros. Fifteen minutes in class; the rest of the deck is a reference.</span>
  </div>
  <div class="aurora-card">
    <span class="aurora-card__icon">🧩</span>
    <span class="aurora-card__title">1 · Compilation &amp; Types</span>
    <span class="aurora-card__desc">Why a pure Python loop is ~100× slower than the same compiled loop, first call vs steady state, the measurement card, and local vs whole-program gain. Tools: <code>@btime</code>, <code>timeit</code>, <code>numba</code>.</span>
  </div>
  <div class="aurora-card">
    <span class="aurora-card__icon">🔀</span>
    <span class="aurora-card__title">2 · Multiple Dispatch vs OOP</span>
    <span class="aurora-card__desc">Julia's multiple dispatch as a language idea, contrasted with Python's OOP / <code>singledispatch</code>. A language module — no parallelism yet.</span>
  </div>
  <div class="aurora-card">
    <span class="aurora-card__icon">🧵</span>
    <span class="aurora-card__title">3 · Threads &amp; Concurrency</span>
    <span class="aurora-card__desc">Concurrency first — <code>@async</code>/<code>@sync</code> to overlap I/O (fetching live market data on one core), then real multithreading with <code>Threads.@spawn</code>: Markov chains and a parallel Monte-Carlo π — including the race condition that silently corrupts a shared counter.</span>
  </div>
  <div class="aurora-card">
    <span class="aurora-card__icon">🧠</span>
    <span class="aurora-card__title">4 · Memory &amp; Batching</span>
    <span class="aurora-card__desc">The processor spends its time <em>waiting</em> for memory. The cache cliff, locality (Julia is column-major — the opposite of numpy), and why <strong>batching</strong> pays by reusing the data already loaded — measured on the CPU, before any GPU.</span>
  </div>
  <div class="aurora-card">
    <span class="aurora-card__icon">⚡</span>
    <span class="aurora-card__title">5 · GPU</span>
    <span class="aurora-card__desc">Thousands of threads — provided you feed them. What the transfer costs, CPU vs GPU matmul, when the GPU starts paying off, and estimating π on the card (CUDA.jl; PyTorch CPU vs CUDA). Coalescing is optional.</span>
  </div>
</div>
```

## Approach

Python is the **common activity track**; Julia provides demonstrations and an optional hands-on route.
Slides frame the reasoning; scripts hold selected demos; Pluto is the executable reference and optional reading.
Use the session plan to select cells rather than running every support in full.
Compare ratios on the **same machine**, recording data types, sizes, warmup and resource counts.
Julia syntax catalogues, detailed SIMD, Markov and manual CUDA kernels are optional.

## Exam

In groups of 2–3: take code from a real project (ENSAI, personal, or open source), speed up one of
its building blocks, and **measure precisely what you gained**. Short report (~8 pages) and
30-minute presentation.

## Activities

20–30 minute activities: predict, complete a small piece of code, check the result, measure and explain.
Python covers every core objective. Julia dispatch is optional. I/O has a labelled simulation fallback;
without a GPU, complete the [GPU analysis route](gpu-fallback.qmd).
